name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
title: Budgets and Allowable Costs
answer: A grant budget is the itemized plan for how money will be spent over the life of a project, and allowable costs are the expenses a sponsor has agreed to reimburse. For AI research the categories are familiar: salaries and fringe for the people doing the work, tuition and stipends for students, equipment, cloud compute and storage, data acquisition and licensing, travel, publication and open access charges, and subawards to collaborators. Each sponsor publishes its own list of what it will and will not pay for, so the same expense can be routine under one program and disallowed under another. The budget is also a statement of scope, because reviewers read it as evidence that the proposed work is feasible at the scale described.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Budgets run on the sponsor's own rules first, then on the institution's pre-award systems. Most universities maintain a sponsored programs office that holds the negotiated indirect cost rate, the payroll and effort reporting systems, and the routing workflow that turns a draft into a submitted proposal. Proposers work in spreadsheets or institutional budgeting modules, then enter the same figures into a sponsor portal, which means the numbers exist in at least two places and have to agree. Cloud and compute estimates often come from a separate vendor quote or an internal research computing group rather than from the budget template itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with the funding opportunity, which sets the ceiling, the period, the cost categories and any cost share requirement. From there a proposer builds the budget line by line, attaches a justification that explains each figure and ties it to a task in the narrative, and checks that the totals match the ceiling and the period of performance. Departmental review, then sponsored programs review, usually follows, and either can send the budget back for revision. Rebudgeting after award is a separate process with its own thresholds, and some shifts between categories need prior approval from the sponsor.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Allowability rests on documentation: a cost is defensible when it is reasonable, allocable to the project, treated consistently and supported by a receipt or a time record. Sponsors audit these records, and institutions carry the risk of disallowed costs, which means the paper trail matters as much as the number. Effort reporting, cost transfers, subrecipient monitoring, conflict of interest disclosure and export control all attach to the budget rather than to the science. Data management and sharing costs, including storage and curation, are increasingly named as allowable, though the terms vary by sponsor and by program.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Compute is the line item most visibly changing, as training runs and inference at scale push cloud and accelerator costs into the same range as personnel on some projects. Sponsors have responded with a mix of dedicated compute supplements, caps on indirect cost recovery, and fixed amount awards that shift the burden of an overrun onto the institution. Open access fees, data curation and the cost of maintaining released models and datasets appear more often in budget guidance than they did a decade ago. The direction is toward budgets justified by a compute and data plan rather than by a staffing table alone.
